To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mutations in the SUR1 subunit of the K(ATP) channel cause opposite effects on channel function and insulin secretion when treated with sulfonylurease chemical chaperones.
the oral hypogylcemic drugs sulphonylureas act as chemical chaperone to rescue the two hyperinsulinemia-associated SUR1 missese mutations R74W and R74E to the cell surface.

two hyperinsulinaemia-associated mutations of the sulfonylureareceptor (SUR1) subunit of the K(ATP) channel, R74Wand E128K, unexpectedly reduce channel inhibition by ATP and that this defect can be rescued to the cell membrane by the oral hypogycemic drug tolbutamide, which acts as a chemical chaperone for K(ATP).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis for the disease phenotypes caused by SUR1 and Kir mutations, and the therapeutic potential of sulfonylures as a treatment for congenital hyperinsulism.
the molecular mechanisms of the ATP-dependent gating of K(ATP) channel and its implication on the pathophysiology of neonatal diabetes and congenital hyperinsulinaemia.
the molecular mechanisms of K(ATP) channel dysfunction in congenital hyperinsulism and neonatal diabetes and how this may be corrected with sulfonylureases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

SUR1 missense mutation E128K and R74W are associated with congenital diabetes, whereas SUR1 mutations E1505K, G1523S, and R2012W are associated with neonate diabetes, and the mutations E128K and E1505K are associated with neonat diabetes and hyperinsulinism.
mutations in SUR1 that cause congenital hyperinsulinaemia are not necessarily associated with neonatal or childhood onset diabetes.

mutations in SUR1 and Kir 6.2 that are expected to cause hyperinsulinism actually cause neonatal diabetes, and that the disease phenotype can be reversed to hyperinsulinism by treating the cells with sulfonylureases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the two hyperinsulinia-associated SUR1 mutations, R74 and E128, are not gain-of-function but rather loss-of-function, and that the disease manifestation is dependent on the expression level of the mutant channels.

mutations in SUR1 that decrease channel function and lead to congenital hyperinsulinaemia are rescued to the cell membrane and cause neonatal diabetes by sulfonylurease, whereas mutations that increase channel function and cause neonatal diaebtes are rescued to the plasma membrane and cause congenital hyperinsuinaemia by sulfonylurase.
SUR1 mutations can cause opposite phenotypes of hyperinsulinism and diabetes, and that chemical chaperones can dictate the manifestation of these phenotypes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

mutations that cause opposite phenotypic outcomes in patients can be rescued to the cell membrane by a single chemical compound and can be made to manifest the opposite phenotype by altering the expression level of the mutant.
the same genetic mutations can cause different disease phenotypes depending on whether the mutant channels are fully expressed or retained in the endoplamic reticulum.
a single genetic defect can cause two opposite disease manifestations depending on whether the channel is rescued to the cell membrane or not.
